Latin.note: Latin joins the population notice in Greek §14 to the honours described in §15. The cut preserves the population subject in §14 and starts §15 at hyrcanum introducing the honours.
The Latin compresses Alexandra’s speech and its contrast between priesthood and kingship; this interval does not reproduce all Greek wording.

The Latin compresses material from Greek XV.39–40 into one removal statement. The phrase praeter legem, corresponding to the statement in Greek §40 that Herod acted unlawfully, occurs earlier and remains in this Latin interval. See the reciprocal note at XV.40.

Partial correspondence: the Latin compresses material from Greek XV.39–40 into one removal statement. Seditiones domesticas pacando corresponds to the household-disturbance phrase within Greek §40. Praeter legem, corresponding to the statement in Greek §40 that Herod acted unlawfully, occurs earlier and remains in the Latin interval assigned to XV.39. This displayed Latin interval supplies only part of the Greek section.
The Latin retains Joseph’s exclusion from Herod’s presence and Alexandra’s confinement; it does not explicitly command Joseph’s execution here as Greek does.
The renewed Arab attack and killings survive; the final Greek escapee statement is shortened in this Latin interval.
The weak/strong contrast survives; Greek’s initial rhetorical question about deeming the enemy brave is not separately expressed in this Latin interval.
The Latin retains Herod’s plan to remove the royal rival but compresses the Greek alternatives concerning his own survival or death.
The reply and promised safe conveyance survive; the Latin shortens the broader Greek promises of assistance.
Hyrcanus’s character and the opening afforded to Antipater and Herod survive; the Greek’s closing explicit verdict of unjust and impious treatment is not separately expressed.
Continued loyalty and counsel survive; the Latin does not separately name Cleopatra or expressly state the killing counsel here. The following interval begins with its counterfactual result.
Restoration of the diadem and honours survive. The Latin recasts Caesar’s letter and does not independently express the Greek gladiator-assistance notice.
The royal reception and army supplies survive; the Latin recasts the Greek account of attendants as a notice of 150 houses. The source wording remains unchanged.
The intensified desire after Mariamne’s death survives; the Greek retrospective account of the earlier passion is compressed.
The repeated calling and attempted distractions survive; the Greek interpretation of divine retribution is not separately expressed.
The notice of killing close friends survives. The four-name enumeration in Greek is not separately expressed in this Latin interval; this section is not absent.
The sons’ influence, fidelity and advocacy survive; the concluding account of their policy is shortened.
The blind conspirator’s readiness to suffer and encouragement survive; his inability to act in the attempt is not separately explained here.
The movement to the theatre and plan to attack Herod survive. The Greek alternative plan to kill others and its intended consequence are not separately expressed.
Ruined crops, exhausted stores and lack of hope survive; the explicit second-year and lost-seed details are shortened.
The opening assessment survives; public hostility and its explanation in Greek are not separately expressed.
Her attraction and the marriage decision survive; Greek’s distinct hearsay and sight stages are compressed.
Roman favour and civic expenditure survive; the Latin compresses Greek’s apology to the Jews and enduring-memorial motive. The outward building location remains in the preceding interval.
The harbour and comparison with Piraeus survive; Greek’s fuller account of the difficult costly construction is shortened.
The harbour-wall towers survive. Greek’s two-hundred-foot construction and distinct wave-breaker account are not separately expressed.
The north-facing entrance survives; Greek’s arches, landing place and promenade are not separately expressed. Section 338 has no independently identifiable Latin interval here.

Text corresponding to this Niese section is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The left-hand foundation tower and the two joined right-hand stone blocks at the harbour entrance have no identifiable counterpart here. The cause is unknown. The north-facing entrance in §337 and the central temple site in §339 survive.

The elevated central temple site, its statues and Caesarea’s name survive. The surrounding dwellings described in Greek are shortened; this temple-attached site is distinct from section 338’s harbour-entry structures.
The Latin gives a compact cave-and-provisions description. It supplies no separately identifiable interval for section 347’s detailed spatial layout.

Text corresponding to this Niese section is unavailable in this Latin transcription. The narrow entrances, spacious interiors, level ground above, and hard rock reached by guided paths have no separately identifiable counterpart here. The cause is unknown. The compact cave-and-provisions description survives in §346, and Herod’s suppression of the brigands survives in §348.
Herod’s receipt of the grant and suppression of brigandage survive; Greek’s opening winding-path and mutual-brigandage details are not separately expressed.
The privileged relationship with Caesar and Agrippa survives; the reciprocal rankings of friendship are compressed.
Roman custody after death survives; Greek’s opening statement that Herod kept the robe there is not separately expressed. The Latin antecedent remains unchanged.
Herod’s strengthening and naming of Antonia survive; the narrator’s explanation of this digression is not separately expressed.
The sanctuary, priest-only inner space and altar survive; Latin does not expressly identify women as excluded at the first inner boundary.
